extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers / reference users (readers of an encyclopedia entry on crypts, cryolite, cryptography, etc.)
extracted.subtask_description: Short encyclopaedia-style reference articles giving historical, architectural and technical descriptions and identification criteria for crypts, cryolite, cryptobranchus, and practical principles and heuristics for cryptography. Entries summarize origins, defining features, notable examples and practical guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cryolite identification and properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Cryolite is a mineral with formula Na3AlF6 (or 3NaF.AlF3), occurring in colourless or snow-white cleavable masses, often tinted brown or red with iron oxide, occasionally black; translucent becoming nearly transparent in water; cleaves in three rectangular directions; crystals occasionally cubic but belong to the anorthic system; hardness 2.5; specific gravity 3; colours a flame yellow (presence of sodium); on heating with sulphuric acid evolves hydrofluoric acid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurrence: almost exclusively at Ivigtut on the Arksut Fjord, S.W. Greenland (large deposit in a granitic vein) and limited occurrences at Ilmen Mountains, Pike's Peak (Colorado), Yellowstone; associated minerals include quartz, siderite, galena, blende, chalcopyrite and alteration products (pachnolite, thomsenolite, ralstonite, gearksutite, arksutite). Economic importance: extensively used as a source of metallic aluminium and as a flux in smelting, in manufacture of certain sodium salts, types of porcelain and glass notable for toughness, and enamelled ware. Note: though called 'ice-stone' (Eisstein) it must not be confused with 'ice-spar' (Eisspath), a vitreous kind of felspar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural definition, origin and primary functions of a crypt
rubrics_metrics.description: A crypt (Lat. crypta) is a vault or subterranean chamber, especially under churches; in early Christian times used for galleries of a catacomb or the catacomb itself and originated in subterranean chapels ('confessiones') erected around the tomb or martyrdom-place of a saint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary objects of construction: (1) to give the altar sufficient elevation so those below can witness sacred mysteries (i.e., the crypt allowed raising the chancel/altar), and (2) to provide a burial place for holy men and relics. The crypt often formed the germ of the church subsequently erected above. The entry includes historical and stylistic notes on how and why crypts were adopted, imitated, or declined in different regions and periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics and notable features used to identify and date cathedral crypts
rubrics_metrics.description: Crypts show characteristic forms and features depending on period and region: many are apsidal; Norman crypts (11th–12th c.) often elaborate with many altars and chapels; some crypts are essentially subterranean churches with multiple altars; Early English crypts show stone groining; Decorated-period crypts may be highly ornamented; examples (Canterbury, Winchester, Worcester, Gloucester, York, Rochester, St Paul's, Westminster) illustrate variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architectural evidence used to date and evaluate crypts includes plan (apsidal vs. nave/aisled reproduction), vaulting type (quadripartite, lierne ribs), pillar forms (clustered shafts, cylindrical, octagonal), presence and arrangement of altars and piscinas, capitals' carving style, and relationship to superstructure. Domestic (secular) crypts: vaulted substructures under merchant houses and guildhalls used as cellars, sometimes mistaken for ecclesiastical vaulting; examples: Guildhall (London), St Mary's Hall (Coventry). Regional examples (France, Germany, Italy, Scotland) cited for comparative identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluative criteria applied to Antonio Diniz's poetry (qualities of good poetry vs. observed faults)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article assesses Diniz's poetic temperament and faults: his imitation of the classics fettered his muse; mythological comparisons and pastoral allegories were poor substitutes for natural feeling; conventionalism prejudiced sincerity; he inwardly believed poetry unworthy of a judge and did not allow his talents full expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific critical observations used as evaluative standards: Anacreontic odes, dithyrambs and idylls won admiration, but Pindaric odes 'lack fire', sonnets are weak, idylls lack truth and simplicity; versification is generally weak and verses 'lack harmony', though his diction is beyond cavil. Guidance implies criteria for good poetry: authenticity/natural feeling, simplicity/truth in idylls, spirited Pindaric tone, strong sonnet construction, harmonious versification, and sincere diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphological and reproductive characteristics for identifying the genus Cryptobranchus
rubrics_metrics.description: Cryptobranchus (family Amphiumidae) are thoroughly aquatic but lung-breathing tailed batrachia characterized by heavy, flattened build; very porous tubercular skin with a frilled fold along each side; short stout limbs with four very short fingers and five very short toes; minute eyes without lids; biconcave vertebrae; ossified gill-arches (two to four) persist though gills are lost in adults; strong series of vomerine teeth across the palate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Species notes: three species known (including fossil Oeningen, Cryptobranchus maximus of Japan/China, and C. alleghaniensis 'hellbender' of North America). Size ranges: fossil and C. maximus over 5 ft; C. alleghaniensis ~18 in. Reproductive traits: eggs laid in rosary-like strings; nesting in deep water holes or clumps; observed parental care (male tending eggs in captivity); larvae hatch ~1 inch long with three branched external gills each side. These morphological and life-history traits serve as identification and natural-history criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bacon's 'virtues' of a good cipher
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon laid down the following as the 'virtues' to be looked for in schemes of cryptography: 'that they be not laborious to write and read; that they be impossible to decipher; and, in some cases, that they be without suspicion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes these principles are more or less disregarded by many modes of cipher, including Bacon's own, and comments on historical reception (Bacon's double cipher praised by some but overstated). These three desiderata form a succinct evaluative rubric for assessing cipher systems: usability (writing/reading effort), secrecy (resistance to deciphering), and stealth (avoid arousing suspicion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency-analysis heuristics for deciphering simple substitution ciphers
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristics recommended for deciphering substitution ciphers: classify letters of the secret message in order of frequency (English letter frequency roughly: e, t, a, o, n, i, r, s, h, d, l, c, w, u, m, f, y, g, p, b, v, k, x, q, j, z). Note common double letters (ee, oo, ff, ll, ss, etc.) and common small words: two-letter words (of, to, in, it, is, be, he, by, or, as, at, an, so); three-letter words (the, and, for, are, but, all, not); four-letter words (that, with, from, have, this, they).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: derive a rough key from letter frequency and common word patterns; familiarity with language composition provides further hints; references to Poe's 'The Gold-Bug' for illustrative technique and to Breithaupt's Ars decifratoria and other treatises for continental-language rules. This provides a practical stepwise rubric for attacking simple frequency-vulnerable ciphers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of cipher types and their properties (substitution, transposition, codes, numeric and arbitrary-character systems)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article describes many classes of cryptographic schemes: simple substitution/transposition (e.g., Julius Caesar shift), Athbash and Albam (Hebrew transposition examples), ciphers in words (codes where classified words represent complete ideas), figures/numerals representing syllables/words/phrases, and the use of shorthand marks or arbitrary characters (historical shorthand, Tiro, Pepys' characters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes on properties and uses: simple substitution is comparatively easy to decipher (frequency vulnerabilities); word-codes (dictionary-classified words representing ideas) are harder and used in telegraphy to both secure message and reduce cost; numerical ciphers can be purposely complicated (historical royal examples deciphered by Wheatstone); shorthand/arbitrary characters are commonly used to represent letters or words and were widely adopted in diplomatic and private correspondence. Historical references and examples (Trithemius, della Porta, Vigenère, Wallis, Wheatstone, Pepys) are provided to illustrate evolution and practical applications.
